auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is a 32px vehicle icon inside the 'Mais Acessados' link to service 2671. The link also shows the same text, 'Emitir o licenciamento anual do veículo (CRLV)', and the live HTML is unchanged. An image inside a link may take an alt that states the link's function, so 1.1.1 does not require the alt to describe the picture. The alt only repeats the visible text. alt="" would be better practice (H2), but that redundancy is not a 1.1.1 failure. The suggested 'Ícone de veículo' would add nothing useful.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is a 32x32 vehicle pictogram inside the 'Mais Acessados' link whose visible text is 'Emitir o licenciamento anual do veículo (CRLV)'. Its alt names the service the icon stands for, which is a functional or symbolic alternative, and WCAG 1.1.1 asks for equivalent purpose, not a description of how the icon looks. The alt repeats the adjacent link text. That is a redundancy issue (H2 or alt="" would be cleaner), but it is not a 1.1.1 failure, and it is not the mismatch the finding claims. The suggested patch, 'Ícone de veículo', would make it worse. The live markup is unchanged.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the featured photo of the 'Ceará em Destaque' bulletin card (a buggy on a sand dune). It is not inside a link, and the h3 directly above it is also 'Ceará em Destaque'. The alt names the publication, not what the photo shows, and the live HTML is the same. If the photo is treated as informative, the alt does not convey its content and the finding holds. If it is an illustration in a card whose information is all in the heading, date and link, it is decorative and the alt is only redundant. That would be at most an F38-style issue, not the inaccurate description the finding claims. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree about whether this photo carries information.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the featured photo of the 'Ceará em Destaque' bulletin card: a buggy on a dune with a beach behind it. It sits directly under the h3 'Ceará em Destaque' and above 'Boletim publicado! 09/10/2026 / Ler boletim'. The image is not a link, and its alt repeats the h3. Competent auditors would split three ways. One reading treats it as an informative photo, so the alt fails as claimed. Another treats it as ambience next to its own heading, in which case the right fix is alt="" (an F38-style issue) rather than a description. A third treats it as the edition's cover image, which is fairly identified by the publication's title. The evidence cannot settle which purpose the photo serves.

ref: #login-button-desktop
subject: Entrar
message: The text "Entrar" has at most 3.42:1 contrast with what is behind it (#fefefe on #22a33e…#1e9f41), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a gradient). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <a id="login-button-desktop" class="btn btn-outline-cc border-2" aria-label="Entrar na área restrita" href="https://acesso.cearadigital.ce.gov.br/login/?app-key=2635e197177591df6014b843c9b85373&origin=https%3A%2F%2Fservicos.ce.gov.br%2F">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the desktop 'Entrar' outline button in the header: white text on the header's green gradient. Sampling the screenshot inside the button gives #21a23e to #24a53a behind #fefefe, about 3.2:1 to 3.4:1. At 20px and weight 400 the text is not large, so it needs 4.5:1, and it fails. The page has an 'Alternar alto contraste' toggle, but G174 does not rescue this. G174 requires the alternate presentation to meet all other criteria, and that mode would keep failures such as the file-name alt on the 'Especiais' banner. So 1.4.3 fails in the default view.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The measurement holds up. The 'Entrar' link in the header is #fefefe text on the green header gradient (about #20a13f behind it). style.css sets .btn-outline-cc to 1.25rem (20px) with font-weight 400 !important, so this is normal-size text needing 4.5:1, and it reaches only about 3.3-3.5:1 in the default presentation. The page, however, offers a visible, focusable 'Ativar alto contraste' toggle in the same header (its icon is about 3.8:1 against the green; it is also bound to Alt+Shift+C). Activating it sets body.contrast-active, and menu-mobile.css then forces the header to #111 with white text, which passes. This is technique G174. Whether that suffices is debatable: G174 needs the control itself to meet the contrast requirement, and it is an icon at 3.8:1, not text at 4.5:1. It also needs the alternate version to conform fully, which this page's other failures make doubtful. Auditors would reasonably disagree, so this is a true positive only if the toggle is not accepted.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the h4 'Boletim publicado!' on the bulletin card, in .text-secondary orange. Sampling the screenshot gives text pixels of exactly #ef6000 on a pale mint gradient (#dff1ef to #e8efee), about 2.83:1. At 24px and weight 500 it counts as large text, so it needs only 3:1, but it still falls short. The live markup is unchanged. The high-contrast toggle does not excuse it, for the same G174 reason as the 'Entrar' button.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The measurement holds up. The h4 'Boletim publicado!' is 24px weight 500 in Kanit, which counts as large text needing 3:1. Its CSS colour is #ef6000 on the light gradient card band (#dff0ee to #e8f0ef), giving 2.81-2.86:1; my own pixel sample was at most 2.92:1. So the default presentation narrowly fails 1.4.3. The page does provide a high-contrast toggle (G174). In that mode, home-for-you.css sets this card band (.for-you-card--last-boletim .bg-active) to background #111 and .text-secondary/.titulo to #fff, which passes easily. Whether that toggle satisfies 1.4.3 is open to debate. Its icon is only about 3.8:1, and G174 requires the alternate version to conform fully, which is doubtful here. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree, so this is a true positive only if the toggle is not accepted.

skeptic.label: true_positive

Rampa's own snapshot name "Senado Federal" is a naming error, but the claim stands. A placeholder alt like "Title" is not an equivalent for a functional logo image (F30). I found no technique that rescues it, and the live page is unchanged.

ref: #header-institucional > div:nth-of-type(1) > nav > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > a
message: When the pointer is over this control (hover), its text has a contrast of 4.37:1 at best with what is behind it, under the 4.5:1 WCAG 1.4.3 asks. Text must keep its contrast in every state a person puts it in; change the hover colors.
evidence: hover: <a> "Fale com o Senado"; changed: color #ffffff → #cccccc, -webkit-text-fill-color #ffffff → #cccccc; #cccccc on #005b9e: 4.37:1 at best, 4.37:1 at worst · 16px, 400
html: Fale com o Senado

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 'Fale com o Senado' link in the dark blue global top bar (nav.navbar_global, background rgb(0,91,158) = #005b9e). I drove the live page in headless Edge at 1280x800 and hovered it. Its color changes from #ffffff to #cccccc (rule ':not(#_) .sf-wrapper .link-deep:hover { color: #ccc }' in essencial.css). Background, opacity, text-shadow and decoration stay the same. The text is 16px at weight 400, so it is not large text and needs 4.5:1. #cccccc on #005b9e works out to 4.37:1, which matches the probe. The rendered crop shows the same solid colors. WCAG 1.4.3 has no exemption for hover states: the hovered text is still text shown to the user, and in that state it falls below 4.5:1. The margin is small but it is a real failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the 'Fale com o Senado' link in the dark blue top bar (16px, weight 400, so not large text). I hovered it on the live page in headless Edge at 1280x800 and waited past its 0.15s color transition. The text settles at #cccccc on the nav's solid #005b9e, with no background image, text-shadow or opacity change. That is 4.37:1 (I recomputed it), under 4.5:1, so it is not a mid-transition artefact. The 1.4.3 Understanding document puts text in hover and focus states in scope. I tried a G174 defence: the page has an 'Alto contraste' toggle, and in that mode this link is white on black. G174 only applies if the alternate presentation conforms, though, and the high-contrast mode has its own 1.4.3 failures: the phone number is #333 on black (1.66:1) and the 24px blue headings are #205c90 on black (2.99:1). So that defence fails and the finding stands. The live page matched the probe on 2026-10-11.

evidence: hover: <a> "Sobre o Senado" (and 5 alike control(s)); changed: color #ffffff → #dddddd, -webkit-text-fill-color #ffffff → #dddddd; #dddddd on #007db8: 3.34:1 at best, 3.34:1 at worst · 16px, 400

On the live page, hover changes the text color from #ffffff to #dddddd (rule ':not(#_) .sf-wrapper .link--nav:hover { color: #ddd }'), and the background stays #007db8. The text is 16px at weight 400, so it needs 4.5:1. #dddddd on #007db8 works out to 3.34:1, which matches the probe. Even the resting white text is only about 4.54:1 there. skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the 'Sobre o Senado' dropdown toggle (#js-menu-0) in the section nav bar, one of six links that share the style. The text is 16px, weight 400. On the live page in headless Edge at 1280x800, hovering changes its color from #ffffff to #dddddd, the end value after the 0.15s transition. The background stays the nav's solid #007db8 (no image or shadow). That gives 3.34:1 (recomputed), well under 4.5:1. At rest, white on #007db8 is only 4.54:1, so hover pushes it below the threshold. Hover state text is in 1.4.3's scope per its Understanding document. The 'Alto contraste' toggle cannot rescue it under G174, because the high-contrast mode itself fails 1.4.3 elsewhere on the page (#333 on black at 1.66:1, 24px blue headings at 2.99:1). auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header's 60-years seal (an SVG reading '60 anos') is the only content of a link to https://60anos.unicamp.br/ (titled 'Home - Unicamp 60 Anos'), and it opens in a new tab. Its alt is 'Selo comemorativo', so the link is announced as 'Selo comemorativo'. That doesn't give the text in the image ('60 anos') or the link's purpose (the site for Unicamp's 60th anniversary), and nothing in the link's programmatic context supplies it. skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The header seal image is the only content of a link to https://60anos.unicamp.br/ (opens the 60-years site in a new tab); the link has no aria-label or title, so its name is the alt "Selo comemorativo". The image visibly reads "60 anos", and the alt carries neither that text nor the destination, so a screen-reader user hears only 'commemorative seal' with no hint of the 60-years site. I looked for a reason it passes (a name on the link, a nearby text label, or an alt naming the anniversary) and found none on the live page. A functional image's alt must describe the link's purpose (H30), so this fails 1.1.1 as the finding says.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the lead news card in 'Notícias Institucionais'. In the live HTML, the <a> wraps the photo (long descriptive alt), the title 'HC celebra 41 anos e homenageia quem construiu sua história' and the excerpt. The link text therefore includes the headline, which exactly matches the destination's title and H1. The finding quotes only the first 300 characters of the alt, which is how the snapshot's AX name is cut off (the cut falls exactly at 300 characters). Rampa's own name field shows the headline. The long alt adds noise, but the link's purpose is clear from its text, so this does not fail 2.4.4.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This news card link goes to the article "HC celebra 41 anos e homenageia quem construiu sua história". Its content is the image (long descriptive alt), then the headline "HC celebra 41 anos e homenageia quem construiu sua história", then the excerpt, so its full accessible name contains the article title. The 'link text' quoted in the finding is the snapshot's browser name, which is exactly 300 characters and stops mid-alt ("...exibindo"). The collector truncated it before the headline. The real link text matches the destination title, so 2.4.4 passes. The long alt that comes first is a verbosity issue, not a 2.4.4 failure.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the Google CSE search box in the header, in a 'search-compressed' container. When collapsed, the input is transparent (opacity 0, per the theme CSS) and is drawn as a magnifying-glass icon (the CSS ::before on .gsib_a), which the screenshot shows at the field's position. Clicking it expands the field and shows the visible label 'Buscar no site'. The Understanding document for 3.3.2 explicitly accepts a magnifying-glass icon as the visible label of a search field, so the claim that nothing on screen says what to enter is wrong. The icon is a CSS pseudo-element and doesn't appear in the snapshot the model judged. Separately, the field doesn't expand on keyboard focus and its outline is removed, which raises a possible 2.4.7 issue, not 3.3.2.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the Google CSE search input in the header, captured in its collapsed state: the input is transparent and a magnifying-glass icon (a CSS ::before on .gsib_a) shows where it is. The theme's all.min.js adds a <label for="gsc-i-id1">Buscar no site</label> after the input. When the box is clicked it gets .search-expand, and the CSS then displays that label as visible text above the field. The input also has title="pesquisar". So there is a visible text label when the field is in use, and the search icon labels it before then. The snapshot did not include either cue (the label is display:none in the collapsed state, and the icon is a pseudo-element), so 'nothing on screen tells what to enter' is not a fair reading of 3.3.2.

subject: ico-escolaridade
message: The text alternative "ico-escolaridade" repeats the image's file name: a screen reader reads it in place of the image. Describe what the image conveys, or use alt="" if it is decorative.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Decorative step illustration (a framed certificate) in the INSCRIÇÃO section, next to text that already says everything: "Informe a escolaridade." Its alt and title are the file name "ico-escolaridade", so a screen reader announces the file name instead of ignoring the image. This is documented failure F30 (file names as text alternatives): a decorative image must be ignorable (alt=""), and an informative one needs a real description. skeptic.label: true_positive

In the live HTML (2026-10-11) the alt is unchanged and neither the image nor any ancestor has aria-hidden or role=presentation, so screen readers announce the file name. The image is arguably decorative, but that does not save it: a decorative image with a non-null alt fails 1.1.1 by F39, and an informative one with a file-name alt fails by F30. No technique makes it pass.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale:
The 'next' link of the news-list pagination: », inside

subject: seu e-mail
message: The placeholder "seu e-mail" has a contrast of 4.45:1 with the field (#757575 on #fbfbfb). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the placeholder "seu e-mail" in the newsletter field. The screenshot pixels confirm placeholder text #757575 (Chrome's default) on a #fbfbfb field background: 4.45:1 for 16px regular text. The placeholder is the only visible cue for what the field wants: the nearby <label for> points to an id that does not exist, and its text is "alertas grátis do Poder360". So it is informative text, it falls under 1.4.3, and it misses 4.5:1, if only narrowly.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Placeholder 'seu e-mail' in the newsletter field. No author ::placeholder rule matches this input (.form-subscribe/widget__modelo2), so Chrome's default #757575 applies, on the field's #fbfbfb background. Both colours appear in screenshot pixels, and the ratio is 4.45:1. The Understanding document for 1.4.3 says it applies to placeholder text, and thresholds are not rounded. Here the placeholder is the field's only visible text cue. Fails 1.4.3, though only narrowly.

subject: #page-885654 > div > div:nth-of-type(9) > form > fieldset > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > a
message: The icon of this link has at most 1.97:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #22d467). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the WhatsApp channel link in the newsletter box: the WhatsApp brand logo (white glyph on WhatsApp green #22d467, on a #fbfbfb box). The 1.97:1 measurement is right, but the Understanding document for 1.4.11 exempts logos under the essential exception and says the exemption carries over to a UI component that is a logo. The logo is shown in its brand colours. Next to it is an "INSCREVA-SE" text link to the same WhatsApp URL. So this is not a 1.4.11 failure; at most it is the best-practice note in the Understanding document.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The link is the WhatsApp logo (icon-whatsapp.svg: white glyph on a green #22d467 circle, close to WhatsApp's brand green #25D366), linking to the Poder360 WhatsApp channel. Understanding 1.4.11 exempts logos under the essential exception, and says this exemption normatively carries over when a logo acts as a control. The brand colours are not an author choice to lower contrast. A separate, readable 'INSCREVA-SE' link right next to it goes to the same URL. Not a 1.4.11 failure.

On a fresh page, Shift+Tab from the first category link ('Musica') lands on Próximo, visible and operable. Its function is also available by keyboard anyway: every product in the carousel is Tab-reachable and scrolls into view on focus, and arrow keys scroll the container. skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The "Próximo" button scrolls the "Novidades" product strip. I checked the live page at 1280x800. It is a native button with no tabindex. Its wrapper turns display:none once the strip reaches its end, and Tabbing through the six product links scrolls the strip there. So a forward walk skips it, and a backward walk run in that same scrolled state skips it too. After a fresh load, Shift+Tab from below does reach it (7th Shift+Tab in my test), so the claim that Tab and Shift+Tab never reach it comes from the state the walk left the strip in. Its function, showing the next products, is also available by keyboard: every product link takes focus and scrolls the strip into view. So 2.1.1 is not failed.

ref: html > body
message: Pressing "d" with focus on the page, and no other key held, changes it: single character key shortcuts that work while no control has focus. Nothing on this page turns them off or remaps them. Let people turn them off, or remap them to include a key such as Ctrl or Alt, or make each work only while its control has focus (WCAG 2.1.4; F99). If a setting elsewhere, such as another page or the account settings, already does this, the criterion is satisfied: waive this finding (rampa waive).
evidence: "d" changed what the window shows; each on two presses with focus on the body, and nothing changed in the same wait with no key

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The claim is that pressing 'd' with focus on the body changes the page. Live at 1280x800 I pressed 'd' repeatedly, and also 'q', 'x', 'a' and no key at all, while logging DOM mutations and screenshot diffs. The only changes in every case came from the countdown digits and the header 'advantages' strip, which rotates on a fixed 3000 ms timer regardless of key presses (rotations at 2611, 5615, 8615, 11613, 14613 ms... with keys pressed in between and no extra change). The only document key listeners are analytics, Sentry and performance wrappers; there are no shortcut handlers. No single-character shortcut exists, so 2.1.4 does not apply. The probe attributed ambient animation to the key press.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The finding is about single-key shortcuts on the body. On the live page, the only key listeners on window, document, html and body are keydown, keypress and keyup on document, all wrapped by the Sentry SDK. With focus on body, pressing "d" (and "x" and "j") changed nothing my checks caught: no scroll, no URL change, no focus move, and no DOM mutation other than the per-second countdown digits and the rotating header-advantages ticker. Those change just the same with no key pressed. The probe's 'changed what the window shows' most likely caught a timer tick, not a shortcut. No evidence of any character-key shortcut.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the department banner, a generic stock photo of open books (banner-departamento.png). The live HTML and CSS show that the white pill reading "Literatura Brasileira" is not part of the image: it is an HTML h2.titulo-sessao placed on top of it, and its bounds in the snapshot match the pill exactly. The image itself has alt="Banner padrão" ("default banner"). That is a CMS placeholder label, not an equivalent for anything the image shows, which is the documented failure F30 (placeholder text used as a text alternative). Because the image is decorative and the heading carries the meaning, alt="Banner padrão" also matches F39, where an image that should be ignored has a non-null alt. Read fairly, the finding's claim that the alt does not match what the image shows names a real 1.1.1 failure. The suggested patch is weak: alt="Literatura Brasileira" would repeat the h2 right beside it, and alt="" is the right fix.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the category header image (banner-departamento.png, a generic stock photo of open books) with alt="Banner padrão", inside an <a> with no href. The white pill reading "Literatura Brasileira" in the model's crop is not part of the image: it is the separate absolutely positioned <h2 class="titulo-sessao"> (bounds 447.9,243.2 384x65.7, matching the pill). The live HTML has the same structure. So the crop misled the model about what the image shows, and the suggested alt "Literatura Brasileira" would only repeat the heading. The image still fails 1.1.1, though. If it is decorative (most likely, since the h2 carries the information), a non-null placeholder alt like "Banner padrão" is failure F39/F30. If it is informative, "default banner" names no content. Either way the claim holds: the text alternative is not a valid alternative for the image. None of my skeptic reasons rescues the element.

ref: #block-portal-fiocruz-branding > div > a
message: At 320 CSS px wide (1280 px at 400% zoom) the page scrolls sideways and this content runs past the right edge: reading it needs scrolling in two directions.
evidence: viewport 320×256 CSS px, page scroll width 360 px; <a> "Início" spans x 12–344 px, 24 px past the right edge (320 px)

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header logo link (img alt "Início", the white FIOCRUZ | CIÊNCIA E SAÚDE PELA VIDA wordmark). I re-ran the page live in headless Edge at 320x256: documentElement.scrollWidth is 360 against a 320 px viewport, so the page scrolls sideways. The overflow comes from the branding block (12-360 px). The logo image is 316 px wide with max-width:none, so it ends at 328 px and the link box ends at 344 px. On screen the tagline reads "CIÊNCIA E SAÚD": the final letter is past the viewport edge. Scrolling right does not bring it back into view, because the orange header background stops at the viewport width and the white letter sits on white. A small overflow, but it is real horizontal scrolling at 320 CSS px that clips content outside any two-dimensional-layout exception. The visible image overflows by 8 px, not the 24 px measured on the link box, but the claim still holds.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the header logo link (an of the FIOCRUZ logotype with the tagline 'Ciência e saúde pela vida', alt 'Início'). I loaded the live page in headless Edge at 320x256 and got the same numbers Rampa did: document scrollWidth is 360, the anchor runs 12-344 px, the image 12-328 px, and its region div (.region-nav-branding) reaches 360 px. That div is what makes the page scroll sideways. The other overflowing boxes are off-screen swiper slides inside a clipped container. The image has max-width:none and renders at a fixed 316 px, so it never shrinks to fit. The last letter of 'SAÚDE' is cut off at the viewport edge. One detail differs from the finding's wording: scrolling sideways does not bring that letter back. The orange header background is only 320 px wide, so the white glyph lands on the white page background. The content is lost, not just reachable by two-way scrolling. Read fairly, the claim (the content does not fit at 320 CSS px and the page scrolls horizontally) is still a real 1.4.10 failure. The overflow is small and the clipped part is a logotype tagline, which makes it low severity, but 1.4.10 has no exception for logos and the image does not need a two-dimensional layout.

ref: #swiper-banner-block-1 > div:nth-of-type(2) > span:nth-of-type(1)
message: This item is marked as the current or selected one (aria-current="true"), and the only thing that shows it is an indicator (#ffffff, inside it) with a contrast of 1.52:1 at most with the colors next to it, under the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 asks of visual information needed to identify a state. Give the indicator 3:1 against what surrounds it, or add a cue in the text (bold, an underline).
evidence: marks taken off: aria-current="true", class "swiper-pagination-bullet-active"; 88 px changed, 88 outside its text, inside it: #ffffff (76 px) next to #bfd6d8 (91%): 1.52:1; its text does not change

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the active pagination bullet (span role=button "Go to slide 1") of the home banner Swiper. I confirmed it live: it carries aria-current="true" and is a 10 px dot in #fff, opacity 1. The other bullets are the same white at opacity 0.5, scaled to 0.66 and 0.33 (dynamic bullets). All of them sit on the slide's light teal strip (#bfd6d8). White on #bfd6d8 is about 1.5:1. The larger size is a non-color cue, but it can only be seen through the dot itself, and the dot is far below the 3:1 that 1.4.11 asks for the visual information identifying this component and its current/selected state. This is the state the slider opens in. Other slides may put the dots on a different background, which could change the ratio, but that does not save the default view.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the active Swiper pagination bullet ('Go to slide 1', role=button, aria-current=true) of the home banner carousel. On the live page, the active bullet is a 10 px white dot at opacity 1. The inactive bullets are the same white at opacity 0.5, drawn smaller (6.6 and 3.3 px dynamic bullets). Nothing else (border, outline, shadow) marks them. The bullets have no background of their own and sit on the slide image. On slide 1, the first slide shown and the one Rampa saw, that image is a light teal bar (#bfd6d8 in the screenshot), and white on it is 1.52:1. I looked for reasons it could pass. The size and opacity differences are all carried by the same white dot, so a low-vision user who cannot see the dot against the bar cannot see the state either. Slide 2 has a dark wooden background with better contrast, but slide 1 (and slide 3, light grey) is a real state of the page and fails. Rampa compared the indicator with its adjacent color, which is the comparison 1.4.11 asks for, not a stricter rule. The visual information that identifies the current-slide state is below 3:1.

ref: #logovlibras
message: Content that appears on hover and on focus covers other content and does not close with Esc. Let people dismiss it without moving the pointer or focus, for example with Esc (WCAG 1.4.13, dismissible; SCR39).
evidence: on hover and on focus, <a> showed <span> "O conteúdo desse portal pode ser acessível em Libras usando…" at x 936, y 32, 184×224 px (position relative), over 7 other element(s) such as <a> "Intranet", <a> "Visite a Fiocruz", <button> "Dislexia"; Esc pressed without moving the pointer or focus: it still showed 600 ms later, and it went away once the pointer and focus left

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The trigger is the gov.br bar's VLibras link (#logovlibras, an empty anchor at the top right). A pure-CSS rule (.logo-vlibras:hover/:focus + .link-vlibras) shows a 184x224 px panel with the VLibras avatar and the text "O conteúdo desse portal pode ser acessível em Libras usando o VLibras". I reproduced it live: the panel appears on both hover and keyboard focus. It covers the Intranet and Visite a Fiocruz links, the Dislexia and Contraste buttons and part of the search field. Pressing Esc while focused, and again while hovering, left it showing; nothing else dismisses it without moving the pointer or focus. It obscures other content and is not an error message, so the dismissible requirement of 1.4.13 fails.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The trigger is the VLibras icon link (#logovlibras) in the gov.br 'Barra Brasil' strip, which is part of the page. Its CSS (:hover/:focus + .link-vlibras) shows a 184x224 px panel with an animated sign-language image, a sentence and a 'VLibras' link. I hovered and focused the trigger in headless Edge. The panel appears at x 936-1120, y 32-256 and is painted on top (z-index 8; elementFromPoint returns the panel). It hides 'Intranet', 'Visite a Fiocruz', 'Dislexia', 'Contraste', 'Inverter' and part of the search field. Pressing Esc did not hide it, either on hover or on focus, and focus stayed on the trigger. It is pure CSS with no script that dismisses it. It is not an input-error message, and it does obscure other content, so neither exception of the dismissible clause applies. The only way to hide it is to move the pointer or focus, which 1.4.13 does not accept. This is a real dismissible failure.

ref: #logovlibras
message: Content that appears when the pointer hovers here disappears when the pointer moves onto it, so someone who magnifies the screen cannot read it (WCAG 1.4.13, hoverable; F95).
evidence: on hover, <a> showed <span> "O conteúdo desse portal pode ser acessível em Libras usando…" at x 936, y 32, 184×224 px (position relative), 0 px from the trigger; the pointer moved onto it in 8 px steps every 16 ms and it disappeared, in 2 of 2 tries

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the same VLibras hover panel. Its CSS does include .link-vlibras:hover, so moving onto it was meant to keep it open. But a decorative full-width div.torres (absolute, from y=30.4 px) overlaps the bottom ~1.6 px of the 32 px trigger, and the panel starts at y=32. I traced it live: moving the pointer straight down from the trigger in 1 px or 2 px steps (a slow, magnifier-style movement) lands on .torres at y 30-32. The trigger loses :hover, the panel collapses during its 0.1 s transition, and at y>=33 the pointer hits the nav underneath, so the panel is gone. Diagonal moves through the same strip fail the same way. Only jumps that skip the strip (or teleporting into the panel) keep it open. Ordinary pointer movement onto the content makes it disappear, so the hoverable requirement fails as the finding says, though the cause is an overlapping layer rather than a missing hover rule.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the same VLibras hover panel. The strongest reason against the finding is that the barra CSS does include '.link-vlibras:hover' to keep the panel open, and with some pointer paths it does stay open. When I moved straight down in 8 px steps from the icon's centre, the panel stayed visible and hovered, which differs from Rampa's 2-of-2 result. Hit-testing shows why both outcomes happen. The page's decorative 'div.torres' (absolute, z-index 0) covers the bottom 2 px of the trigger (y 30-31). A pointer there hovers neither the trigger nor the panel, so the panel switches at once to display:block/height:0, collapses and turns hidden. Slow straight-down moves of 1, 2, 3 and 5 px per frame, and Rampa-style 8 px steps aimed at the panel's centre, all made it disappear. Only paths that happen to jump over the 2 px band keep it open. Slow pointer movement is typical of screen-magnifier users, the group this clause protects. Moving the pointer onto the panel often makes it vanish, so it is not reliably hoverable (F95). The finding names a real 1.4.13 failure, even though whether a given try fails depends on the pointer path.

subject: hidden svg
message: This image is hidden from screen readers (an svg with no name), but it conveys what the text around it does not say: "Logo naming the organizations: "TUA SAÚDE | REDE D'OR"".
evidence: Logo naming the organizations: "TUA SAÚDE | REDE D'OR"

patch.ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(6) > div > section > nav > svg
patch.to: Logotipos da Tua Saúde e Rede D'Or.
patch.after: <svg class="icon icon-logo-tuasaude-rdor " aria-label="Logotipos da Tua Saúde e Rede D'Or.">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Inline SVG co-brand logo 'TUA SAÚDE | REDE D'OR' that heads the footer find-a-doctor nav. The live HTML has no title, aria-label or role on it, and the AX tree exposes it as an unnamed image. The nav's own text (city and insurer links, 'Disponível em...') never says this is a Rede D'Or partner service, so the logo carries information that has no text alternative, which is a 1.1.1 failure. One correction: the message says 'hidden from screen readers', but the SVG is not aria-hidden. It is exposed as an image with no name. The substance of the claim, a meaningful image with no text alternative, still holds.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Inline <svg class="icon-logo-tuasaude-rdor"> at the top of the 'Encontre um médico' link list (footer banner): the '+ TUA SAÚDE | REDE D'OR' co-brand logo. Live HTML confirms it has no title, aria-label, role or aria-hidden; the snapshot exposes it as an unnamed image. Looked for a reason it could be decorative: nothing else in this section (title 'Encontre um médico por cidade', the city/insurer links, the 'Disponível em' disclaimer) names Tua Saúde or Rede D'Or, so the logo is the only cue that this doctor-finder is a Tua Saúde/Rede D'Or service. The header's 'Uma marca Rede D'Or' tagline is far away and does not make this image redundant. An informative logo with no text alternative fails 1.1.1; 'hidden' is loose wording (it is exposed without a name), but the claim holds.

ref: #newsletter-footer > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > input:nth-of-type(1)
message: The field "Digite seu email" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing. Chromium's own form check flags this field too.

patch.ref: #newsletter-footer > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > input:nth-of-type(1)
patch.before: <input name="email" required="" type="email" class="input" placeholder="Digite seu email">
patch.after: <input name="email" required="" type="email" class="input" placeholder="Digite seu email" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Newsletter footer input (type=email, name=email, placeholder 'Digite seu email') collects the user's own email address, which is one of the input purposes listed for 1.3.5. Both the snapshot and the live HTML show no autocomplete attribute, so the purpose is not programmatically identified (H98 is not met). Under 1.3.5, type=email alone is not accepted as identifying the purpose. Real failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Newsletter field <input type="email" name="email" placeholder="Digite seu email"> in the footer form 'Se inscreva na nossa newsletter'. It asks for the user's own email address, a listed input purpose. Neither the snapshot nor the live HTML (re-checked 2026-10-11) has an autocomplete attribute, and Chromium raised its autocomplete form issue for it. type="email" gives the data format, not that the address is the user's own, and the only sufficient technique for 1.3.5 is autocomplete (H98). No passing technique applies.

subject: Dúvidas comuns
message: The text "Dúvidas comuns" has at most 3.23:1 contrast with what is behind it (#8f8f8f on #ffffff), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (an element over or under it). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: 'Dúvidas comuns' is the last link in the article's anchor tabs. Site CSS sets .article-anchors ul li a to var(--gray-60) = #8f8f8f on a white background, at 16px weight 400. That is 3.23:1, below the 4.5:1 required. The screenshot shows it as gray text, partly faded under the 'next' gradient button, which only lowers its contrast further. The sibling tab links use the same color, so the measurement is not an artefact. Real 1.4.3 failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: 'Dúvidas comuns' link in the article's in-page anchor bar. Live CSS: .article-anchors ul li a {color: var(--gray-60)} = #8f8f8f, 16px weight 400, on the white header background. #8f8f8f on #fff is 3.23:1, below 4.5:1, and the snapshot's pixel measurement agrees. Possible objection: the item is partly clipped by the overflow container and the 'next' button's fade. That does not exempt it, because it is real link text that is fully shown once the bar scrolls, and the other anchor links share the same failing color. No exception (inactive, decorative, logotype) applies.

ref: #newsletter-footer > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > input:nth-of-type(1)
subject: Digite seu email
message: The placeholder "Digite seu email" has a contrast of 2.52:1 with the field (#a3a3a3 on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input name="email" required="" type="email" class="input" placeholder="Digite seu email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The newsletter email field's placeholder 'Digite seu email' is #a3a3a3 (var(--gray-50) via .input::placeholder) on the .input white background, 14px weight 400. That is 2.52:1, below 4.5:1. The field has no visible label, so the placeholder is the only on-screen text that says what to type. It is visible text with no 1.4.3 exception (the control is active), so it fails 1.4.3.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Placeholder 'Digite seu email' of the footer newsletter email field. Live CSS: .input::placeholder {color: var(--gray-50)} = #a3a3a3 on a white field, 14px weight 400: 2.52:1, below 4.5:1, matching the snapshot. Possible objection: placeholders are not required to meet contrast. That does not hold here. 1.4.3 has no placeholder exception, the field is not inactive, and the placeholder is the field's only visible label and its accessible name, so it is information users need.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
subject: compartilhe
message: The icon of this link ("compartilhe") has at most 1.98:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #25d366). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the WhatsApp share link in the left share bar: a white WhatsApp glyph on a #25d366 circle (class 'green'). The ratio 1.98:1 is measured correctly. However, #25d366 with a white glyph is WhatsApp's own brand logo presentation. The 1.4.11 Understanding document places logos under the 'essential' exception and says the exemption carries over normatively when the logo is used as a user interface component. Giving it more contrast is only a best practice there. The low contrast comes from the brand colors, not from a design choice by this site, so this is not a 1.4.11 failure as WCAG defines it. The rule applied G207 without the logo exception.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: WhatsApp share link (aria-label 'compartilhe'): a white WhatsApp glyph in a 24px circle with background #25d366 (live CSS .article-share ... a.green). White on #25d366 is 1.98:1 (recomputed), and the green circle against the white page is also 1.98:1, so the control's only visual has low contrast. However, the glyph is the WhatsApp brand logo in its official colorway, and the 1.4.11 Understanding exempts logos (the essential exception). It only advises a higher-contrast variant when a logo acts as a UI component, and is not exempt when the low contrast is the author's choice. Auditors reasonably split on social-media brand icons, so this is not settled.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: 'Próximo item' is the scroll button for the article anchor tabs, visible at desktop width; the screenshot shows a small blue '>' caret. Its only visible content is the caret SVG in var(--primary-60) = #36b1df on the button's white gradient over a white page, which is 2.47:1. The caret is the only thing that shows the control is there and what it does, and it is not a logo, so it needs 3:1 under 1.4.11. Real failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: 'Próximo item' button in the article anchor bar: its only visible content is an SVG caret with fill currentColor. Live CSS: .article-anchors .navigator-wrapper {color: var(--primary-60)} = #36b1df. The caret sits on the white end of the button's transparent-to-white gradient, so the adjacent color is #ffffff: 2.47:1, below the 3:1 that 1.4.11 asks for the graphic that identifies a control. Possible objections fail: the caret is not a logo, nothing else visually identifies the control, and it is the mouse user's way to reveal the clipped anchors (the container is overflow:hidden at desktop).

ref: #header > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > label
subject: LabelText click,keydown
message: This element ("Busca IA do Tua Saúde") takes keyboard focus and listens to click, keydown, so it works as a control, but the browser exposes it as LabelText, with no control role: a screen reader does not announce it as a button or a link (F59). Use the native element (button, a) or give it the role of the control it is.
evidence: role LabelText · click, keydown · "Busca IA do Tua Saúde"

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header 'Busca IA do Tua Saúde' trigger is a <label for=headerSearch tabindex=0> with click and keydown listeners. The input it points to sits inside a hidden search container, so this label is the only way to open the search overlay. Chrome exposes it as LabelText with an empty computed name and no button or link role. Native labels do not respond to Enter, so the keyboard behavior is scripted. This is a scripted custom control whose role is not programmatically determinable (F59 pattern), so 4.1.2 fails. A <button> or role=button would fix it.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Header '<label tabindex="0" for="headerSearch" class="search">Busca IA do Tua Saúde</label>'. The snapshot shows the real search form container (.header-tuasaude-search-container) hidden, so this focusable label, with click and keydown listeners, is the visible trigger that opens the AI search. Chrome exposes it as LabelText with no control role and an empty name of its own. A screen reader user who reaches it hears only text, not a button. Its native label behavior (focusing #headerSearch) cannot be what makes it work while that input is hidden. A scripted, focusable control with no role is the F59 pattern, so it fails 4.1.2 as reported.

ref: #body-page > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > img

The alt names exactly the institution the image shows: "Pinacoteca" is its common name and also the page's h1. So the claim that the alt describes something the image does not show is wrong. skeptic.rationale: The element is the header logo image (alt="Pinacoteca") inside the home link, which also carries a visually hidden "Ir para a página inicial". The crop the model saw, and the page screenshot, show the wordmark "PINACOTECA DE SÃO PAULO", so the image does show "Pinacoteca". The finding's claim that the alt describes something the image does not show is false. "Pinacoteca" is the museum's common short name (it is also the page's h1) and serves the logo's purpose. At most the alt is shorter than the wordmark, which is not a 1.1.1 failure. The model had the crop and judged it wrongly.

The snapshot HTML and the live page fetched on 2026-10-11 have no autocomplete attribute on the input or the form (the string "autocomplete" does not occur anywhere in the page). ref: #rodape > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > a
subject: Logotipo Hous 360
message: The icon of this link ("Logotipo Hous 360") has at most 2.21:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#abaeb9 on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
html: <a href="http://hous360.com.br/" target="_blank" title="Desenvolvido por Hous360. Será aberto em uma nova aba.">

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: This is the footer credit link to Hous360, the site's developer. Its only visible content is an SVG of the Hous logotype, with fill #575d73 inside a group set to opacity="0.5", so it renders about #abaeb9 on white. I computed 2.21:1, so the measurement is right, and the crop shows a faint grey logo. Logos and logotypes fall under 1.4.11's essential exception, and the Understanding document says that exemption normatively carries over to a control whose only content is a logo. But the same document says a logo that normally has enough contrast loses the exemption when an author chooses to show it with low contrast. Here #575d73 at full opacity would be about 6.5:1, and the 50% fade is hard-coded in the theme, but I cannot tell whether it comes from Hous360's brand guidelines. Competent auditors would reasonably split on this. The finding also calls the logo an "icon" (G207), which understates the logo question.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the footer "developed by" link to hous360.com.br. Its only visible content is an inline SVG logo whose paths are filled #575d73 inside <g opacity="0.5">. That renders exactly #abaeb9 on the white bar, about 2.2:1, matching the rule's measurement and the screenshot. The obvious defence is the logo exemption. However, the WCAG 2.2 Understanding for 1.4.11 says a logo presented at low contrast as an author choice, not because of brand colours, is not 'essential' and is not exempt. Here the brand colour #575d73 (about 6.5:1) is deliberately faded to 50% opacity, and no hover or focus style restores it (theme CSS checked). The logo is all that identifies the link, so it fails 1.4.11.

ref: #menu-item-294 > a
subject: Visita
message: The link text "Visita" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

patch.ref: #menu-item-294 > a
patch.before: Visita
patch.after: Visite a Pina Educação

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: "Visita" is a top-level main-menu dropdown toggle (href="#", data-bs-toggle="dropdown", aria-haspopup, aria-expanded=false; the accessibility tree reports hasPopup=menu). It opens a submenu: Ingresso, Como chegar, Planeje sua visita, Grupos agendados, Acessibilidade. Its purpose, opening the "Visita" section menu, is clear from its text together with its programmatically determined context (the menu list item and its popup state). The packet gave the model that context, so 2.4.4 is met. The suggested text "Visite a Pina Educação" is also wrong. If anything is at issue, it is that a dropdown toggle is exposed as a link rather than a button (4.1.2), not link purpose.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: "Visita" is a top-level main-menu item with href="#", data-bs-toggle="dropdown", aria-haspopup and aria-expanded=false. The accessibility tree exposes hasPopup=menu, collapsed. It does not go anywhere: it opens the "Visita" submenu (Ingresso, Como chegar, Planeje sua visita, Grupos agendados, Acessibilidade). Its text plus its programmatic context (a navigation list item and the popup state) makes that purpose clear, which satisfies 2.4.4. The finding judges it as if it were a navigation link to a destination. Exposing a toggle as a link rather than a button would be a 4.1.2 role question, not 2.4.4. The model had the dropdown-toggle HTML and the submenu text in the ancestors.

ref: #menu-item-297 > a
subject: Pina
message: The link text "Pina" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

patch.ref: #menu-item-297 > a
patch.before: Pina
patch.after: Pina Educação

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: "Pina" is a top-level main-menu dropdown toggle (href="#", data-bs-toggle="dropdown", aria-haspopup, aria-expanded=false). It opens the section about the museum: O museu, Acervo, Biblioteca, Conservação e Restauro, Apoie, Gestão and more. "Pina" is the museum's own short name and is used throughout the page ("Pina nas redes sociais", "ingressos da Pina"). With its menu context, the purpose of opening the Pina section is determinable, so 2.4.4 is met. The suggested "Pina Educação" would mislabel it, since Educação is a separate menu.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: "Pina" is a main-menu dropdown toggle (href="#", data-bs-toggle="dropdown", aria-haspopup, aria-expanded=false; the accessibility tree has hasPopup=menu). It opens a submenu about the museum (O museu, Acervo, Biblioteca, Conservação e Restauro, Gestão...). "Pina" is the museum's own nickname, used across the page (e.g. "Pina nas redes sociais"). Its purpose, opening the Pina section menu, is determinable from the text and its programmatic context, so 2.4.4 is met. The suggested rename "Pina Educação" is even wrong, since Educação is a separate menu. The model had the HTML and the submenu text.

ref: #rodape > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > a
subject: link
message: The browser exposes this element as a link but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "link", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the footer logo link to https://www.cultura.sp.gov.br/. Its only content is an image of the São Paulo state government crest ("Governo do Estado de São Paulo, Secretaria da Cultura"), which has alt="", and the link has no aria-label, title or other text. The accessibility tree shows a link with no name, and the live page has the same markup. A screen reader announces only "link", so the link fails 4.1.2 (and 2.4.4 and 1.1.1 by F89). The sibling logo links in that row have the same problem.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is a footer link to https://www.cultura.sp.gov.br/ whose only content is an image (the São Paulo government / Secretaria da Cultura crest) with alt="". There is no title, aria-label or text, and it is focusable and not hidden. The browser's accessibility tree gives the link no name, and the live HTML on 2026-10-11 is the same. This is documented failure F89 (also 2.4.4): screen readers announce just "link". The other logo links in the same row share the defect. Nearby text links do not name this link, so no passing technique applies.

ref: #web-messenger-container |> #footer > form > div > textarea
subject: Enviar
message: The label "Enviar" does not say what to enter.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the message textarea of the 'Lina do Metrô' chat widget (Smooch, inside an iframe). It was collapsed at capture (bounds null) but appears when the user opens the chat, so it is page content. Its accessible name comes from title="Enviar" ('Send'), which takes precedence over placeholder="Digite uma mensagem...". A screen reader user therefore hears the field announced as 'Enviar'. That describes the send action, not what to type, and makes the field sound like a button. The label given to assistive technology does not describe the field's purpose, which is what 2.4.6 requires. Only the visible placeholder is descriptive. This also bears on 4.1.2. The live chat widget is injected by script, so I could not re-check it with a fetch.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the message textarea of the third-party Smooch/Zendesk chat widget ("Lina do Metrô"), inside an iframe. The widget was closed when Rampa read the page: the textarea had no bounds and only the launcher button showed. The textarea gets its accessible name "Enviar" from a title attribute that the widget fills with its sendButtonText setting (seen in the live page's config). Its visible placeholder is "Digite uma mensagem..." ("Type a message..."), which does say what to enter. Arguments against a 2.4.6 failure: the identifier shown to sighted users is descriptive, and "Enviar" appears only as a hover tooltip and in the programmatic name. On that reading, the mismatch is better filed under 4.1.2 or 2.5.3. The argument for it: screen reader users get "Enviar" ("Send") as the field's label, which names the button's action rather than what to type. Competent auditors would split on whether that is a 2.4.6 label failure, so I label it uncertain.

The name starts with the visible label and names exactly that destination, so it matches where the link leads. They are imprecise about what a click does at desktop width, which at most is a minor naming (4.1.2) or best-practice note, not a 2.4.4 failure. Rampa had the destination title and still judged that the name does not match it, so the cause is model_error.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the 'Economy' item in the primary site navigation, a link to /economy with aria-label 'Economy sub menu toggle'. auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header navigation link 'Gaeilge' leads to the Irish-language site (index.ga.php). It is the name of the language written in Irish, and the live HTML has no lang attribute on it, so it inherits html lang="en". The Understanding document for 3.1.2 uses this exact case as its example ('Alternative language links': each language name, written in that language, carries a lang attribute). The language change is clearly intended, so the single-word and vernacular exceptions do not reasonably apply. This is a 3.1.2 failure.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is the header language-switcher link "Gaeilge" (to the Irish version). Neither the link nor any ancestor has a lang attribute, so it inherits lang="en"; the live page is the same. Marking language-switcher endonyms with lang is common practice, and here a change of language is clearly intended. But the Understanding document for 3.1.2 exempts proper names, and a language's name arguably is one. It also says single words should be treated as part of the surrounding language unless a change is clearly intended. And 'Gaeilge' is in everyday Hiberno-English use; the site's own English text uses Irish terms such as 'Gaeltacht' unmarked. Competent auditors split on single-word language-switcher links, so I cannot call this a clear failure.

subject: Skip to navigation
message: The link text "Skip to navigation" does not match where the link leads: "News".

patch.before: Skip to navigation
patch.after: Skip to News

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: Offscreen skip link 'Skip to navigation' with href="#navigation". In the snapshot the id 'navigation' is on the first link of the main navigation (the 'News' pillar link), so the link does move the user to the site navigation, exactly as its text says. The model took the name of the target element ('News') for the link's destination; landing on the first nav item is what skipping to navigation means. The link text describes its purpose; no 2.4.4 failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: A skip link, 'Skip to navigation', with href="#navigation". In the snapshot, #navigation is the 'News' link, the first item of the primary navigation. The link does just what its text says: it moves to the start of the site navigation. The model mistook the name of the first nav item for where the link goes. The text describes the purpose exactly, so this is not a 2.4.4 failure, and 'Skip to News' would be less accurate.

auditor.rationale: Header sub-navigation link 'UK' (href /uk-news, destination title 'Latest UK news | The Guardian') inside a nav list of news sections: World, US politics, UK, Climate crisis, Middle East, Ukraine, Environment... On a news site's section navigation, a link named 'UK' among other section names clearly leads to the UK news section, and the destination confirms it. skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The 'UK' link (href /uk-news) is one item in the header's News sub-navigation list: World, US politics, UK, Climate crisis, Middle East, Ukraine, and so on, inside the nav landmark. The model had that list and the destination title ('Latest UK news | The Guardian'). On a news site's section bar, 'UK' plainly means the UK news section, just as 'World' means world news, and the link goes there. The purpose can be told from the link text and its nav/list context, so this is no 2.4.4 failure. 'UK news' would be clearer, but that is advice, not a failure.

skeptic.rationale: The 'Learn more' link comes right after the h3 'Deeply read', inside the text 'What readers are spending time with (Learn more)' (snapshot readingText of its container). It goes to 'What is the Deeply read list'. Its purpose follows from the link text with its programmatically determined context: the same sentence/parenthetical and the preceding heading (sufficient technique H80, also G53). The model had both the heading and the surrounding text. It passes 2.4.4 (it would only be an AAA 2.4.9 issue).

ref: #checkbox-id-masthead-edition
subject: Int
message: The label "Int" does not say what to enter.

patch.ref: #bannerandheader > header > gu-island > nav > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > label
patch.after: <label for="checkbox-id-masthead-edition" class="dcr-1lscl6k">Include in masthead</label>

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The element is the masthead edition picker: a visually clipped checkbox (tabindex=-1) labelled by a visible <label> 'Int' that toggles a hidden list of edition links (International, UK, US, Australia, Europe edition); the live HTML is the same. The finding's framing is off: it is a disclosure toggle, nothing is 'entered', and the patch ('Include in masthead') shows the model misread the control. Read fairly, though, the claim is that 'Int' does not describe the control's purpose, and that is arguable: 'Int' is a cryptic abbreviation of the current edition and says nothing about choosing an edition, so a screen reader hears 'Int, checkbox, not checked'. Others would pass it as the established visual edition-switcher pattern and file the real problems under 4.1.2 (checkbox role for a menu button) and 2.1.1. Competent auditors would disagree on the 2.4.6 call.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The element is the Guardian masthead edition picker: a visually hidden checkbox (1x1, clipped, tabindex=-1) used as a CSS toggle, labelled by a visible <label>Int</label>, which opens a list 'International edition / UK edition / US edition / Australia edition / Europe edition'. The live page has the same markup. The finding's wording ('does not say what to enter') and its patch ('Include in masthead') show the model misread it as a data-entry checkbox. Nothing is entered here, and 'Int' does name the current edition. Still, the abbreviation 'Int' does not say that this control switches edition, and a screen reader hears 'Int, checkbox, not checked'. The bigger problem there is the role (4.1.2), not the label's wording. Auditors could reasonably go either way on whether 'Int' is a descriptive enough label for 2.4.6.

ref: #container-food > gu-island > div > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > h3
subject: unmarked|en|tarte Vaudoise à la creme
message: This passage has no lang attribute, so it is read as English (en), but it is in French (fr).

patch.ref: #container-food > gu-island > div > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > h3
patch.after: tarte Vaudoise à la creme

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The h3 card headline 'Henry Harris' recipe for tarte Vaudoise à la creme' (Food section) has no lang markup, so the French dish name is read with English rules. 3.1.2 exempts proper names and words that have become part of the surrounding vernacular. 'Tarte vaudoise à la crème' is not English vernacular, and a strict auditor would ask for lang="fr" on the multi-word French phrase. Many others treat a dish's name in an English recipe headline as a name, which needs no language change, and the passage is short and still understandable. The evidence does not settle which reading applies; competent auditors would reasonably disagree.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is the h3 of a Food card, 'Dessert / Henry Harris’ recipe for tarte Vaudoise à la creme'. Neither the h3 nor any ancestor below <html lang="en"> has a lang attribute (the live page is the same), so a screen reader will say the French dish name with English rules. But 3.1.2 exempts proper names, technical terms and phrases that have entered the vernacular. A regional dish name in an English recipe headline ('tarte Vaudoise', capitalised as a name; 'à la crème' close to the naturalised 'à la carte') can be read as a culinary name/term rather than a passage in French. Competent auditors disagree on whether dish names like this need lang markup, so I can't settle it either way.

ref: #newsletter-signup-email-1
message: The field "Email Address:" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing. Chromium's own form check flags this field too.

patch.ref: #newsletter-signup-email-1
patch.before: <input class="newsletter-signup__input svelte-m7l5d3" type="email" placeholder="Your email address" id="newsletter-signup-email-1" name="email" required="">
patch.after: <input class="newsletter-signup__input svelte-m7l5d3" type="email" placeholder="Your email address" id="newsletter-signup-email-1" name="email" required="" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the footer newsletter sign-up field, an input type="email" with a visually hidden label "Email Address:". It collects the user's own email address, which is one of the WCAG input purposes. The snapshot has no autocomplete attribute anywhere on the page. The live HTML fetched on 2026-10-11 has the same markup (only the id suffix differs) and still no autocomplete. type="email" gives the data type, not the input purpose, so nothing makes the purpose programmatically determinable. That fails 1.3.5 as the finding says.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the footer newsletter sign-up input (type=email, name=email, a visually hidden label 'Email Address:', posts to signup.propublica.org). It asks for the user's own email address, which is an input purpose listed in WCAG 1.3.5. The snapshot and the live HTML fetched on 2026-10-11 both show no autocomplete attribute, and Chromium flagged the same thing. type=email only sets the data format and does not identify the purpose, and no ARIA or other mechanism does either. I looked for a reason it passes (for example, the address belonging to someone else, or autocomplete being added by script) and found none. Fails 1.3.5.

ref: #bottom-panel-cta-email
message: The field "Please enter your email address:" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing. Chromium's own form check flags this field too.

patch.ref: #bottom-panel-cta-email
patch.before: <input type="email" name="email" id="bottom-panel-cta-email" class="bottom-panel-cta__email svelte-1dz4e5r" placeholder="you@example.com" required="">
patch.after: <input type="email" name="email" id="bottom-panel-cta-email" class="bottom-panel-cta__email svelte-1dz4e5r" placeholder="you@example.com" required="" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the bottom-panel newsletter call-to-action field, an input type="email" with the visually hidden label "Please enter your email address:" and the placeholder you@example.com. It asks for the user's own email address and has no autocomplete attribute, both in the snapshot and in the live HTML (no autocomplete appears anywhere on the page). Nothing else identifies the purpose programmatically, so it fails 1.3.5.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the email input in the bottom-panel newsletter CTA ('Get the Newsletter'), with type=email, name=email and placeholder you@example.com. It collects the user's own email address, but neither the snapshot nor the live HTML has autocomplete=email, and Chromium's form check flagged it. type=email does not identify the purpose under 1.3.5, the sufficient technique is H98 (autocomplete), and nothing else on the element supplies the purpose. The claim holds.

ref: #main > article > div > div > p:nth-of-type(71) > a
subject: nearly a quarter of all Americans
message: The link text "nearly a quarter of all Americans" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.
evidence: nearly a quarter of all Americans

patch.ref: #main > article > div > div > p:nth-of-type(71) > a
patch.from: nearly a quarter of all Americans
patch.to: Read more about the statistics on Americans with active sports betting accounts
patch.after: Read more about the statistics on Americans with active sports betting accounts

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is an inline citation link in the article body. The live HTML reads: "Today, nearly a quarter of all Americans, and half of men ages 18 to 49, say they have an active sportsbook account, according to the Siena Research Institute." Under 2.4.4, the purpose of a link can be determined from the link text together with its programmatically determined context, and the enclosing sentence and paragraph count as that context. Here the sentence makes clear that the link leads to the Siena Research Institute source for the statistic, and the href (sri.siena.edu) matches. The paragraph text was in the packet's ancestor context, so the model had what it needed and judged wrongly.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is an in-article citation link. The live sentence reads 'Today, [nearly a quarter of all Americans], and half of men ages 18 to 49, say they have an active sportsbook account, according to the Siena Research Institute.' The link goes to the Siena Research Institute release on that statistic. 2.4.4 accepts link purpose that can be determined from the link text together with its programmatically determined context (the same sentence or paragraph, technique G53). Here the sentence names the source being cited, so the purpose is clear. The model had the paragraph text, including 'according to the Siena Research Institute', even though the collector moved the link text to the end of it, and it still judged wrongly.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > footer > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > section:nth-of-type(1) > h2
subject: INFO
message: The heading "INFO" says nothing about the content under it.

patch.ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > footer > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > section:nth-of-type(1) > h2
patch.after: About and Navigation

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the footer h2 "Info" (shown in uppercase by CSS), heading a list of links to About, Impact, Leadership, Staff, Partners, Awards, Events, Jobs and Fellowships. Its sibling footer headings are Coverage, Local, Contact and Support us. "Info" is short, but it describes the topic of the group: information about the organization. 2.4.6 requires headings to describe their topic or purpose, not to be detailed or exhaustive. The packet showed the section content, so this is a wrong judgment, not missing context. Competent auditors would pass this footer column heading.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is a footer column h2 'Info' (styled uppercase) above the links About, Impact, Leadership, Staff, Partners, Awards, Events, Jobs and Fellowships. Its sibling headings are Coverage, Local, Contact and Support us. In that context 'Info' accurately names the group as information about the organization. 2.4.6 asks only that headings describe their topic or purpose, and the Understanding document says they can be short. A terse, conventional footer category label like this is not a 2.4.6 failure, and the claim that it 'says nothing about the content under it' is wrong. The model had the section's link text. The suggested replacement is a preference, not a WCAG requirement.

ref: #bottom-panel-cta-email
subject: Please enter your email address:

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The label of the bottom-panel email field is "Please enter your email address:" (a label element with for=bottom-panel-cta-email, visually hidden with class p-a11y). It says exactly what to enter: an email address. The suggested fix, "Email address", says the same thing. The label describes the field's purpose, so 2.4.6 is met. Any problem caused by the label being visually hidden would belong to 3.3.2, not to this claim.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The label 'Please enter your email address:' is a visually hidden label (class p-a11y) programmatically tied to the type=email newsletter input. It states exactly what to enter, an email address, so the claim that it 'does not say what to enter' is plainly wrong, and the suggested 'Email address' says the same thing. The label being visually hidden, with only the placeholder you@example.com showing, might be worth looking at under 3.3.2 or 2.5.3, but it is not a 2.4.6 failure of the label's descriptiveness.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > img
subject: oma-with-cookies

patch.ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > img

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The cookie-banner illustration (crop and src oma_with_thomann_cookies.png) shows a cartoon grandmother holding a tray of cookies. 'Oma' is German for grandma, so alt="oma-with-cookies" describes exactly what the image shows. It is clumsy, filename-like and partly German, and the image is arguably decorative, so alt="" might be better. But the finding's claim, that the alt describes something the image does not show, is wrong. The model seems not to have understood 'oma'.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the cartoon image in the cookie consent banner. The crop shows a grandmother ("Oma" is German for grandma) holding a tray of cookies, so alt="oma-with-cookies" describes exactly what the image shows. The suggested patch says the same thing in English. The claim that the alt describes something the image does not show is wrong. The image is decorative and alt="" would be better, and the alt is clumsy and comes from the filename. But a correct, non-misleading description is not a 1.1.1 failure. The live page is unchanged.

ref: #main > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > img
subject: Days Money-Back
message: The text alternative "Days Money-Back" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: #main > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The USP badge icon is an image of text reading '30 DAYS' in a hexagon. Its alt is 'Days Money-Back', and the link's visible text is also only 'Days Money-Back' (confirmed in the screenshot and on the live page). The number 30, the actual guarantee period, exists only as pixels and is missing from the text alternative, so the alt is not equivalent to the image. The finding's wording (the alt describes something not shown) is loose, but its claim that the alt does not match the image holds. The patch ('30 Days Money-Back') fixes exactly that, so it is a real 1.1.1 failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is a USP badge link: an icon reading "30 DAYS", then a visible span "Days Money-Back". The image alt is "Days Money-Back", so the link's accessible name is "Days Money-Back Days Money-Back" (snapshot AX tree). The number 30 appears only in the image, and no alt, title or hidden text supplies it. The text alternative does not match the image of text and drops the key fact, which is a real 1.1.1 failure. The finding's wording is loose (the real gap is the missing "30", not invented content), but its claim of an alt/image mismatch holds, and its patch "30 Days Money-Back" names the fix. The live page still has the same markup.

ref: #main > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > a > img

skeptic.rationale: This is the same badge pattern: the icon reads "3 YEARS", and both the alt and the adjacent span say "Years warranty". The link name is "Years warranty Years warranty", so the 3 conveyed by the image of text is not available programmatically anywhere. The alt is not equivalent to the image, so 1.1.1 fails. ref: #main > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > a > img
subject: Free Shipping Over
message: The text alternative "Free Shipping Over" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: #main > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > a > img

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The badge image is a plain delivery-truck icon inside a link whose visible text is 'Free Shipping Over £149'. Its alt, 'Free Shipping Over ', states the icon's purpose (shipping) rather than its appearance, which 1.1.1 allows for functional images. Unlike the 30-days and 3-years badges, the icon carries no information that the visible text lacks. At worst the alt is redundant with the link text (alt="" would be cleaner), which is not a 1.1.1 failure. The suggested 'Delivery truck icon' reflects a literal-description requirement that WCAG does not impose.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The icon is a delivery truck inside a link whose visible text is "Free Shipping Over £149", and its alt is "Free Shipping Over ". A truck icon stands for shipping, so a functional alt naming the shipping offer is acceptable. The icon adds no information beyond the adjacent text. Repeating the text is redundant (alt="" would be cleaner), but redundancy is not a 1.1.1 failure. The model asked for a description of the image's appearance (its patch: "Delivery truck icon"), which is not what 1.1.1 requires for a functional icon.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > button:nth-of-type(1) > span
subject: Alright!
message: The text "Alright!" has at most 1.69:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #13e47c), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a pseudo-element). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The 'Alright!' text on the cookie banner's primary accept button is 18px bold, which is below the 18.66px bold large-text threshold, so it needs 4.5:1. The live CSS confirms '.cookie-consent-spice .consent-button--primary{background:#13e47c; color:#fff}' (the wrapper does have class cookie-consent-spice), which gives about 1.69:1. That fails even the 3:1 large-text threshold. The banner is shown on load, and the measurement matches the stylesheet. Real 1.4.3 failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the "Alright!" accept button in the cookie consent banner. The live stylesheet (vendor-fx.css) confirms the colours: `.cookie-consent-spice .consent-button--primary{background:#13e47c;color:var(--fx-color--neutral-white)}`. White on #13e47c works out to 1.69:1. The text is 18px bold (13.5pt bold), below the large-text threshold, so 4.5:1 applies. It would also fail the 3:1 large-text minimum. It is real text on an active control, so the incidental and logotype exceptions do not apply. The full-page screenshot does not show the banner, but the snapshot captured it and the live CSS confirms the colours.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div > h4
subject: Served with love!
message: The heading "Served with love!" says nothing about the content under it.

patch.ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div > h4

auditor.rationale: The h4 'Served with love!' heads the cookie-consent banner, whose content asks the user to accept cookies for preferences, statistics and marketing. skeptic.rationale: This is the h4 "Served with love!" in the cookie consent banner. ref: #groupie-carousel-headline
subject: In Your Own Words

ref: #bfc23f60-3a4c-11f1-97aa-3fa1bfb68f96 > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a
subject: Explore now
message: The link text "Explore now" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

patch.after: Explore dining furniture by style

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The 'Explore now' button-styled link is one of only two children of the teaser header container (div.pub__teaser__info-container); the other is the h2 'How would you like to explore? By style, feature, size or shape', shown right beside it in the screenshot. The destination page, 'Dining Furniture By Style', with the description 'Explore all dining furniture by style, feature, size or shape', matches that. The claim that nothing around the link tells where it goes is wrong. skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the 'Explore now' button in the teaser at the top of the page. In the snapshot it sits in the same pub__teaser__info-container as the h2 'How would you like to explore? By style, feature, size or shape', and that heading comes immediately before it. The screenshot shows them side by side as one unit. auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: 'Here's how you know' toggle (a role=button). The link is in the gov banner: 12px Poppins weight 300 text on white.
