auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The Featured Topics button 'Food Safety Tips for Dining Out' (47px tall). I replayed the backward walk on the live page at 1280x800: focus the last element, then Shift+Tab. Shift+Tab #54 puts focus on it, and the browser scrolls it to y = -0.3..46.7. The body > nav header is position: fixed, 0-74px. All 25 elementFromPoint grid points over the button hit the nav, and the viewport screenshot shows no part of the button. html has no scroll-padding-top. The focused component is entirely hidden by author-created sticky content. That is the documented failure F110 of 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), as the finding says.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Featured Topics button 'Food Safety Tips for Dining Out' (47px tall). The probe's backward walk had focus on 'A' at scrollY 944; Shift+Tab then scrolls this button to the top edge (scrollY 931, y 0). I reproduced this live in headless Edge: the navbar 'navbar fixed-top navbar-on-scroll' (opaque #005ea2 background, 74px tall) slides in at top:0 when the page scrolls up, and 0 of 25 grid points on the focused button hit the button; the screenshot shows only the blue nav and white space below it, with no part of the button or its focus ring visible. There is no scroll-padding, and nothing the user opened. The focused control is entirely hidden by author content, which is the sticky-header case that 2.4.11 targets. It only happens when moving backward from that scroll position, but focus arriving that way is a normal way to reach the control.

ref: #topic > article > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > span:nth-of-type(4) > a > img
subject: X
message: The text alternative "X" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

patch.ref: #topic > article > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > span:nth-of-type(4) > a > img

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the X logo, the only content of a share link (mplus-share.js builds it as ; clicking opens a tweet-intent window). It sits in the page-actions row beside the title, next to 'Email this page to a friend', Print, Facebook, Pinterest and RSS icons. The alt 'X' names the service the logo shows, so it gives the same information a sighted user gets from the icon, and the link is not unnamed (F89 does not apply). The finding says the alt 'does not say where the link leads'. That is a link-purpose (2.4.4) concern, and a best-practice wish for 'Share on X'. It is not a 1.1.1 failure: the text alternative is equivalent to the image.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the X logo image (alt="X", link title="X", href="#") in the share row beside the h1, between siblings named "Email this page to a friend", "Print", "Facebook", "Pinterest" and "Subscribe to RSS". auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The live markup is Español with no lang attribute, inside . 'Español' is a Spanish word, the name of the target language in a language switcher. message: This link in a block of text is told apart from the text around it only by its color, and that color has a luminance contrast of 1.56:1 with the text, under 3:1 (F73). Underline it, or give it another cue that does not rely on color (WCAG 1.4.1; G183).
evidence: <a> "Managing Diabetes": link #006699 against text #444444, 1.56:1; no underline, border, weight, style, icon or pseudo-element sets it apart at rest

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The link "Managing Diabetes" is the title at the start of a bullet in a MedlinePlus resource list ("Start Here"). Each bullet reads: title link, NIH icon, then the source organization in parentheses, with "Also in Spanish" on a second line. On the live page the title is #006699, 14px, regular weight, with no underline at rest (underline only on hover). The visible text next to it is not the li's #444444, which is what the rule compared against. It is span.orgs/desc-text in #666666 at 12px. The color contrast is under 3:1 either way (about 1.1:1 against the gray annotation), but color is not the only cue. The link is the item's title, set larger (14px against 12px) and in its own position, ahead of a smaller parenthetical attribution. That is the "visually evident from page design and context" case F73 sets apart from links inside prose, much like the titles of a list of search results. The finding says "only by its color", but it checked underline, border, weight, style and icon and ignored the font-size difference and the list layout. That applies F73/G183's inline-text-link test more strictly than SC 1.4.1 requires. The trailing "Spanish" link (12px, same size as "Also in") would be a stronger 1.4.1 case, but it is not this finding. This is borderline, and a strict auditor might still flag it.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The 'Managing Diabetes' link is the title at the start of a bulleted resource-list item ("Start Here"); the item goes on with an NIH badge image, then the source organisation in parentheses (span.desc-text), then "Also in Spanish" on its own line. On the live page (headless Edge, 1280 px) the link is #006699 at 14px with no underline at rest (underline only on hover), but the text next to it is not #444444 at the same size, as the evidence implies: #444444 is the li color, which colors no visible text; the adjacent text is #666666 at 12px. So the link is set apart by a larger font size as well as by color, and is further separated by the badge image and the parentheses. That is exactly G182 example 3 (a list of article links with extra information, links not underlined but in a larger font than the rest), a sufficient technique for 1.4.1; F73 itself says links can be evident from page design and context, and this is a list-item title, not a link inside running text. The rule only counts underline, border, weight, style, icons and pseudo-elements, not font size, so it applied a stricter test than WCAG. (The "Spanish" link in "Also in Spanish" is a closer F73 case, but it is not the element reported here.)

ref: #mplus-search > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > button
message: When the pointer is over this control (hover), its text has a contrast of 3.46:1 at best with what is behind it, under the 4.5:1 WCAG 1.4.3 asks. Text must keep its contrast in every state a person puts it in; change the hover colors.
evidence: hover: <button> "GO"; changed: background-image linear-gradient(rgb(50, 158, 57) 0%, rgb(43, 135, 55) 25%, rgb(33, 102, 46) 100%) → linear-gradient(rgb(50, 158, 57) 75%, rgb(43, 135, 55) 100%); #ffffff on #329e39…#319e38: 3.46:1 at best, 3.45:1 at worst · 14px, 700
html: <button class="form-btn" title="Search MedlinePlus" alt="Search MedlinePlus" type="submit">GO</button>

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header search submit button "GO" has white text, 14px bold. That is not large text (bold large text starts at 14pt, about 18.7px), so 4.5:1 applies. In the live page at rest, the background is a gradient (#329e39 to #2b8737 at 25% to #21662e), and the text, which runs from about 29% to 71% of the button height, sits on about #2b8737 or darker, roughly 4.5:1 or more. On hover the gradient changes to linear-gradient(#329e39 75%, #2b8737 100%), so the whole text sits on #329e39. White on #329e39 is 3.45:1, which I computed myself and which matches the probe. There is no text-shadow or other aid. Text in a state the user puts it in (hover) falls below 4.5:1, so this fails 1.4.3 as reported.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The search "GO" submit button has white text, 14px bold, which counts as normal-size text (bold large text starts at 18.66px), so it needs 4.5:1. On the live page the hover rule swaps the background to linear-gradient(#329e39 75%, #2b8737 100%), so the whole glyph area (centre of a 38px button) sits on solid #329e39. White on #329e39 is 3.45:1, and there is no text-shadow or other aid. At rest the darker gradient passes. The Understanding document for 1.4.3 says it applies to text shown while a pointer hovers over an object, and no exception (inactive, incidental, logotype) applies. I found no reason the claim fails: real 1.4.3 failure in the hover state.

ref: #searchtext_primary
message: When this element has keyboard focus, its focus indicator (#f7fbfe, #deeefa, around it) has a contrast of 2.00:1 at most with the colors next to it, under the 3:1 that WCAG 1.4.11 asks of visual information needed to identify a state. Give the indicator a color with at least 3:1 against what surrounds it, such as an outline of 2 px that is dark on a light page.
evidence: Tab ×6: <input> "Search MedlinePlus" focused and blurred; 5701 px of its indicator around it: #f7fbfe (3625 px) next to #fafcfe (61%), #deeefa (32%): 1.14:1; #deeefa (1356 px) next to #f7fbfe (67%), #66afe9 (32%): 2.00:1; style sheet: border-top-color #66afe9, border-right-color #66afe9, border-bottom-color #66afe9, border-left-color #66afe9, box-shadow #00000013, box-shadow #66afe999
html: <input id="searchtext_primary" class="form-text" type="text" placeholder="Search MedlinePlus" alt="#Site Search input" title="Site Search input" maxlength="400" size="40" name="query" autocomplete="off" role="textbox" aria-autocomplete="list" aria-haspopup="true">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header search text input (#searchtext_primary). On keyboard focus (reached with 6 Tabs on the live page), the author style sets outline 0, changes the 1px border from #b4b4b4 to #66afe9 and adds a soft rgba(102,175,233,.6) glow. These pixels are indeed under 3:1 against white (the border is about 2.4:1 and the glow is lower), as the probe says. However, this is a text input: on focus it shows the text caret in caret-color #444444 (inherited from color), about 9.7:1 on the white field. The Understanding document for 1.4.11 (Figure 33, 'Text input focus style') rules this exact pattern a pass: a faint author outline (#CCC, 1.6:1) plus the visible caret, because the caret "does provide a sufficiently strong visual indication". Only a low-contrast custom caret fails (Figure 44), and that is not the case here. The probe measured only the ring and ignored the caret, so it applied a stricter test than 1.4.11 requires.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the "Search MedlinePlus" text input (#searchtext_primary). On focus it gets a Bootstrap-style #66afe9 border and a pale blue glow, with outline none. The probe is right that these are under 3:1 (the #66afe9 border is 2.37:1 on white; the glow is lighter). But this is a text input: when it gets focus it shows the native text caret, which keeps the default color (caret-color auto = #444444, 9.7:1 on the white field). The 1.4.11 Understanding document (Figure 33, "Text input focus style") passes exactly this case: a faint outline under 3:1 plus a visible caret, because the caret is a strong enough focus indication. It fails only when the caret is customised to low contrast (Figure 44), which is not so here. The probe compares screenshots, which normally hide the blinking caret, and then requires the styled ring to reach 3:1 by itself. That is stricter than what the criterion requires.

ref: #content > div > article > h2
subject: Everything for
message: The heading "Everything for" says nothing about the content under it.

patch.ref: #content > div > article > h2
patch.after: Research Business Schools

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is an h2 with the text 'Everything for', followed by three link tiles: Research, Business and Schools (to /hubs/research, /hubs/business and /hubs/schools). Visually, the heading reads as the start of a phrase that the tiles finish. As a heading, though, 'Everything for' is a dangling fragment. In a headings list, or when jumping by heading, it reads as 'Everything for, heading level 2' and says nothing about the section's topic (audience hubs for researchers, businesses and schools). 2.4.6 requires headings to describe the topic or purpose of their section, and this one does not without the visual layout that follows. Some auditors would accept it as a stylistic lead-in, so it is a low-severity call, but I judge it a real failure as reported. The suggested replacement, 'Research Business Schools', is a poor fix (something like 'Everything for research, business and schools' would be better), but that does not change the label. The live page still has the same h2.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: h2 'Everything for' sits directly above three large card links: Research, Business and Schools (hub pages). On screen it reads as a lead-in that the cards complete ('Everything for Research / Business / Schools'), and the site uses the same label for the same link group in its navigation. The live page has the same markup, with no hidden text. Read with the cards that follow, the heading does tell you this is a set of audience hubs, and 2.4.6 allows short headings that give an appropriate cue. Out of context, though (in a screen reader's headings list, for example), 'Everything for' is a dangling fragment that names no topic. Competent auditors could reasonably call this either a pass or a weak-heading failure, so I cannot confirm it as a true positive. The suggested patch is also poor.

In that state the backdrop blocks the pointer and Tab is trapped inside the dialog, so no user can put the button into that focus state. In every state a user can reach, the text meets 1.4.3.

skeptic.rationale: The element is the secondary 'All events' button link below the event cards. On the live page I tabbed onto it in headless Edge. ref: #ccc-close
message: When this element has keyboard focus, its focus indicator (#5a5853, around it) has a contrast of 1.78:1 at most with the colors next to it, under the 3:1 that WCAG 1.4.11 asks of visual information needed to identify a state. Give the indicator a color with at least 3:1 against what surrounds it, such as an outline of 2 px that is dark on a light page.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 'Close cookie control' X button on the dark (#313147) cookie banner. The site uses the floating-focus library: on keyboard focus an author-styled div draws a 2px #5a5853 border (var(--color-text-tertiary)), 2px outside the button, and the native outline is suppressed (.floating-focused {outline-style:none}). I compared live screenshots before and after focus, after the helper flash had faded. The only change is 240 px of #5a5853 surrounded on both sides by #313147, which is 1.78:1. It is not a user-agent default indicator, it is the only thing that shows the focused state, and it is under the 3:1 that the 1.4.11 Understanding asks of focus indicators against adjacent colours.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the 'Close cookie control' X button in the CIVIC cookie panel, a dark #313147 slide-out. After any keyboard use the site enables floating-focus-a11y, which removes the element's outline and draws a floating 2 px border in the outline colour, rgb(90,88,83) = #5a5853 (var(--color-text-tertiary)), 2 px outside the button. I confirmed on the live page that the floating element's border is solid 2px #5a5853 and that the button's computed outline-style is none. The ring has only panel colour on both sides, and #5a5853 against #313147 is 1.78:1. Once the transient overlay fades, nothing else marks focus. The UA-default exception does not apply because the author replaced the default ring; that default is only visible when the panel auto-focuses the button on load, before any key is pressed. This matches the Understanding 1.4.11 case of an external indicator that does not contrast with the adjacent background.

#content > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > div > p; shown with an ellipsis

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the description in the 'Treasures of the British Library' card. The whole card is a link to events.bl.uk/exhibitions/treasures-of-the-british-library. With the WCAG spacing values on the live page, the paragraph's 3-line clamp drops its 4th line ('...in our... [permanent exhibition.]'), as reported. The design clamps the same text at 1024, 900, 768, 600 and 320 px even without spacing. The 1.4.12 Understanding ('Use of ellipses') says truncation still meets the criterion when the ellipsis is in a section with a link and the linked page reveals the text. The linked page says the gallery 'displays some of the world's most exciting, beautiful and significant books, manuscripts...' and calls it 'our free permanent gallery', so no content is lost. Rampa never read the destination.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the teaser description in the 'Treasures of the British Library' card. The paragraph is inside the card's link to events.bl.uk/exhibitions/treasures-of-the-british-library and is styled with -webkit-line-clamp: 3 and an ellipsis. Live at 1280 px with WCAG text spacing, the paragraph needs 4 lines and the last words ('our permanent exhibition.') become an ellipsis, so the measurement is right. However, Understanding 1.4.12 ('Use of ellipses') says a page still conforms 'where the ellipsis is part of a section of content which includes a link, the truncated text is revealed on the linked page'. Rampa never read the destination. That page says the gallery is a 'free permanent gallery' displaying 'some of the world's most exciting, beautiful and significant books, manuscripts...', so the hidden content is available there. The same clamp also cuts the text at 1024 px with no text spacing, which shows it is a deliberate teaser convention. A strict auditor might want the exact sentence, but the documented link allowance applies.

skeptic.rationale: Footer image link (no aria-label) to /en/support/donate/anbi-information; its only content is the ANBI logo with alt "ANBIlogo". The extra word 'logo' is noise and 'ANBI information' would be better, but requiring the alt to spell out the destination more than the visible logo does is stricter than 1.1.1 (H30 is satisfied when the alt conveys the link's purpose, which 'ANBI' does here).

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(2) > form > button

message: The text "Accept" has at most 4.13:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #d55140), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a background image). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <button data-bind="css: { 'button-disabled':busy }" class="button-bold button-primary button-combo-end button-forward" name="gdprChoice" value="Accept" type="submit">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The cookie bar's 'Accept' button is 15px bold white text on .button-primary {background-color:#d55140}, confirmed in the live CSS and in the screenshot pixels. White on #d55140 is 4.13:1. 15px bold is not large text (that needs 18.66px bold), so 4.5:1 is required and the button fails 1.4.3.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The cookie banner's Accept button: white 15px bold text on the button's solid background. The site CSS sets .button-primary to background-color #d55140, and the screenshot pixels around the label are #d55140 (the banner is not dimmed). White on #d55140 is 4.13:1; 15px bold is not large text (needs 18.66px bold), so 4.5:1 applies. The background-image is only the small arrow sprite. Fails 1.4.3.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The header 'Login' link is 17.2px regular white text over the hero painting, under only a light header::before gradient (opacity 0.45). Against white that is about 3.3:1 to 4:1, well below the 4.5:1 that normal-size text needs, and no text-shadow is applied. This fails 1.4.3.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Header 'Login' link: white 17.2px regular text laid directly over the hero painting (the swan's light wing). The measured background #838072-#afac94 gives 2.3-3.97:1, below 4.5:1 even at its darkest; the undimmed strip of the swan at the top of the screenshot is of the same light tone (about #a19c83), and the site CSS adds no text-shadow or scrim for .link-2020-inverse. The screenshot itself is dimmed by the cookie overlay, but in that state the text is dimmed too, and in the normal state the background is lighter, so either way it fails 1.4.3.

ref: html
subject: Keep me informed
message: The page title "Keep me informed" says nothing about this page.

patch.ref: html
patch.after: <title>Newsletter Sign-up - Rijksmuseum</title>

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The <title> 'Keep me informed' is the same as the H1 and states the page's purpose: signing up to be kept informed, that is, the newsletter. WCAG 2.4.2 asks for a title that describes the topic or purpose. It does not require the site name, although adding 'Rijksmuseum' or 'newsletter' would help. The claim that the title 'says nothing about this page' is not accurate. This is not a 2.4.2 failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The document title is 'Keep me informed', identical to the page's h1, on a page whose sole content is a newsletter sign-up ('Sign me up for the general English newsletter'). The title states the page's purpose, which is what 2.4.2 asks; it lacks the site name, but WCAG does not require one (adding it is advisory). The finding's claim that it 'says nothing about this page' does not hold; the suggested 'Newsletter Sign-up - Rijksmuseum' is a best-practice improvement, not a fix for a failure.

auditor.rationale: The footer social link to the museum's YouTube channel has aria-label 'Youtubelink' and contains the YouTube logo. Its name says the link goes to YouTube, and its context (the site footer's social icon row) shows it is the Rijksmuseum's channel. The purpose is clear from the link text and its context, so it does not fail 2.4.4.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: Footer social link to the Rijksmuseum YouTube channel with aria-label 'Youtubelink', the YouTube icon as its only content, sitting in the row with Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and LinkedIn links on the Rijksmuseum site. The name says it goes to YouTube, which, in the footer of the museum's site, identifies the museum's YouTube presence; the run-together wording is clumsy but the purpose is clear. The claim that it does not tell where the link goes is wrong; no 2.4.4 failure.

ref: #NewsletterSubscription_Preposition
subject: Preposition
message: The label "Preposition" does not say what to enter.

patch.ref: #maincontent > section > form > div:nth-of-type(1) > section > fieldset > ol > li:nth-of-type(3) > label
patch.after: <label for="NewsletterSubscription_Preposition" class="block-left align-label-input sixth-page-fixed tablet-sm-1col tablet-sm-stack-compact">Enter a preposition (e.g., 'at' or 'in')</label>

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: The optional field between 'Firstname' and 'Lastname*' is labelled 'Preposition'. It is a literal translation of the Dutch 'tussenvoegsel', meaning surname particles such as 'van' or 'de'. An English user unfamiliar with Dutch names may not know what to enter, so the claim has some merit. But its position in the name sequence gives a clue, and auditors rarely fail 2.4.6 over a translation choice, so competent auditors could disagree. The suggested patch ('e.g., at or in') misreads the field.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: Optional text field labelled 'Preposition' between Firstname and Lastname*: an English rendering of the Dutch 'tussenvoegsel' (name particles such as 'van', 'de'). In that position many users will infer it is part of the name, and the label does name what it wants; but 'Preposition' is not the usual English term for a name particle and an English speaker unfamiliar with Dutch names could read it as grammar, as the model's own patch ('at' or 'in') did. Whether that makes the label non-descriptive under 2.4.6 is a judgment call on which competent auditors would disagree.
